summary: This function runs lazydocker (a Docker management tool) inside a container, configured to see the current folder's compose.yaml file. It first checks that Docker is installed and that the lazydocker image exists locally, offering helpful instructions if either is missing. Then it launches the container with proper volume mounts so lazydocker can access Docker, your project files, and optional configuration.

explanations.6: This stores the Docker image name in a variable so we can reference it consistently throughout the function.
explanations.8: This is the directory where the Dockerfile and compose.yaml files live on your computer, used for rebuilding the image if needed.
explanations.11: This is the same path but shown as a literal string (with ${HOME} unexpanded) so when we print error messages, users can copy-paste the command exactly as written.
explanations.12: This is the path inside the container where lazydocker stores its configuration files, so we can mount a volume there.
explanations.14: This checks whether the docker command exists on your system; if it doesn't, the function stops immediately with an error.
explanations.15: The escape codes (\e[31m and \e[0m) make the error text appear in red; >&2 sends the message to stderr (error output) instead of stdout.
explanations.19: This checks if the lazydocker Docker image has already been built on this machine; if not, we show instructions on how to build it.
explanations.35: This creates an empty array that will optionally hold volume mount flags if a config file exists.
explanations.37: If a custom config file is found, we add the volume mount syntax to the array so it gets passed to docker run.
explanations.40: The --rm flag deletes the container after it exits, -it keeps it interactive with a terminal attached, and the -v flags mount volumes.
explanations.43: This unpacks the config_mount array into the docker run command; if the array is empty, nothing gets added, but if it has content, it gets inserted here.
